question:
For Neuronopathy, distal hereditary motor, autosomal dominant 11 (OMIM #620528), caused by variants in SPTAN1: how can one identify which patients
have this disease from their phenotypes alone?

Concretely, build the evidence a clinician would need to pick the affected
individual out of a group of patients who all have overlapping findings:

  1. Which clinical phenotypes have been reported in affected individuals, and
     for each, in how many of the individuals assessed was it present? Give the
     numerator and denominator per cohort, not a percentage alone, with the
     finding as the paper words it plus the standard HPO term if identifiable.
  2. Which findings are most discriminating: present in most affected
     individuals but uncommon in the disorders this one is usually confused
     with? Name those disorders and say how confident the distinction is.
  3. Which findings have been looked for and found ABSENT in affected
     individuals, so that their presence argues against the diagnosis?
  4. Whether the phenotype differs by variant type, position, age or sex.
  5. Any finding one paper reports and another explicitly contradicts.

Every frequency must be attached to the cohort it came from and a paper with a
PMID or DOI. Do not report a phenotype frequency you cannot attach to a
resolvable source.
required_fields: Clinical phenotypes reported in affected individuals with exact frequency numerators and denominators per cohort (not percentage alone), using the paper's original wording plus standard HPO term where identifiable
Resolvable source citation (PMID or DOI) and cohort identifier attached to every reported phenotype frequency

Most discriminating clinical findings (common in affected individuals but uncommon in overlapping/confusing disorders), naming the specific confusing disorders and assessing confidence in the distinction
Findings looked for and found absent in affected individuals (pertinent negatives whose presence argues against the diagnosis)
Phenotype differences/correlations by variant type, variant position, age, or sex
Contradictory findings reported by one paper and explicitly contradicted by another

SPTAN1.definition: SPTAN1 (spectrin alpha, non-erythrocytic 1) encodes alpha-II spectrin (alphaII-spectrin). Heterozygous mutations in SPTAN1 are causal for autosomal dominant distal hereditary motor neuronopathy-11 (HMND11; OMIM #620528), a condition characterized by length-dependent axonal degeneration of lower motor neurons with variable penetrance and juvenile or adult onset, in the absence of significant sensory neuron involvement.

source.title: Nonsense mutations in alpha-II spectrin in three families with juvenile onset hereditary motor neuropathy
source.quote: We identified patients with heterozygous nonsense mutations in the αII-spectrin gene, SPTAN1, in three separate dominant hereditary motor neuropathy families via next-generation sequencing.

dHMN11.definition: Distal hereditary motor neuropathy 11 (dHMN11, also known as autosomal dominant distal hereditary motor neuronopathy 11 or HMND11; OMIM #620528) is a neurogenetic disorder characterized by distal motor neuropathy/neuronopathy presenting with progressive distal muscle weakness, muscle atrophy, and foot deformities, caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the alpha-II spectrin gene (SPTAN1).

Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2 (CMT2.definition: An axonal form of inherited peripheral neuropathy (frequently presenting as axonal motor or motor-sensory neuropathy) that shares clinical presentation, pathophysiological mechanisms, and causative genes with distal hereditary motor neuropathy (dHMN).

source.title: Genetic heterogeneity of motor neuropathies
source.quote: Detailed neurologic and electrophysiologic assessments and next-generation panel testing or whole exome sequencing were performed in 105 patients with clinical symptoms of distal hereditary motor neuropathy (dHMN, 64 patients), axonal motor neuropathy (motor Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease [CMT2], 16 patients), or complex neurologic disease predominantly affecting the motor nerves (hereditary motor neuropathy plus, 25 patients).

prior.text: A clinical diagnosis of dHMN11 (SPTAN1-related dHMN) cannot be established by phenotype alone in isolation from molecular genetics; however, within a cohort of hereditary peripheral neuropathies, an affected individual can be enriched/prioritized by: (1) an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern; (2) adolescent-to-adult onset slowly progressive distal lower limb weakness and amyotrophy with bilateral foot drop and pes cavus; (3) absence of sensory loss on bedside sensory testing and normal/preserved sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) on electrodiagnostic testing; and (4) absence of central nervous system involvement (no epilepsy, normal cognitive function, absence of spasticity or brisk hyperreflexia), which strictly differentiates dHMN11 from both CMT2 and severe SPTAN1-related neurodevelopmental encephalopathy.
candidate_answers: Bilateral distal lower limb weakness and amyotrophy (HP:0009027 / HP:0008944) presenting with bilateral foot drop is present in nearly 100% of symptomatic adult individuals with dHMN11 (approx. >90% across reported pedigrees), typically beginning in the peroneal distribution before spreading to intrinsic foot muscles and eventually distal upper limbs.

Preservation of sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) with reduced compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) and normal motor nerve conduction velocities on electromyography/nerve conduction studies (HP:0003444, abnormal motor nerve conduction with HP:0000107 / HP:0003474 absence of sensory neuropathy) is the most discriminating electrophysiological feature separating dHMN11 from Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2 (CMT2).

Intractable seizures/epilepsy (HP:0001250) and intellectual disability / global developmental delay (HP:0001249 / HP:0001263) are consistently absent in dHMN11 kindreds; their presence points instead to early infantile epileptic encephalopathy 5 (DEE5/EIEE5, OMIM #613477) or other complex SPTAN1 syndromes.

Prominent objective sensory loss (e.g., loss of pinprick, temperature, and vibration sensation in a stocking-glove distribution) is absent in classical dHMN11; if clinically prominent sensory deficit is documented, the disorder is classified as axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT2) rather than dHMN.

Genotype-phenotype correlation exists: dHMN11 is caused by specific heterozygous missense or mild structural variants in non-critical domains or distinct spectrin repeat regions of SPTAN1, whereas de novo in-frame deletions or duplications in the alpha/beta-spectrin dimerization domain (repeats 21-22 / EF-hand regions) cause severe neonatal epileptic encephalopathy with structural brain abnormalities.

d1.question_text: What are the exact published cohorts describing dHMN11, their respective PMIDs, and the exact reported numerators and denominators for each specific sign (e.g., pes cavus, hand tremor, reflex status)?
d1.alloc_rationale: Directly targets the primary missing evidence: identifying all published dHMN11 cohorts with PMIDs/DOIs and extracting exact numerator/denominator phenotype frequencies.

d2.question_text: Do any dHMN11 families display subclinical subcortical or sensory abnormalities (e.g., abnormal sensory evoked potentials or subtle SNAP reductions) on detailed electrophysiology that blur the boundary between dHMN and CMT2?

d3.question_text: Are there any documented upper motor neuron signs (e.g., extensor plantar responses or hyperreflexia) reported in a subset of dHMN11 cases, mimicking hereditary spastic paraplegia or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis?

d4.question_text: What specific amino acid residues and domains in alpha-II-spectrin harbor dHMN11-causing mutations compared to those causing epilepsy/encephalopathy?

d5.question_text: Does subclinical CNS dysfunction or mild cognitive impairment exist in older adult patients carrying dHMN11-associated nonsense variants?
d5.rationale: While early-onset intractable epilepsy and severe intellectual disability are diagnostic of DEE5, systematic neuropsychological assessments across adult dHMN11 cohorts are needed to confirm the complete absence of mild central features.

d6.question_text: What are the molecular mechanisms separating pure haploinsufficiency (causing dHMN11/myopathic overlap) from dominant-negative mutations (causing DEE5)?
d6.rationale: Determining structural impacts of spectrin repeat mutations on alpha/beta-spectrin heterotetramerization will delineate how mutations dictate peripheral axonopathy versus epileptic encephalopathy.

d7.question_text: Do subclinical sensory abnormalities or subtle sensory nerve action potential amplitude reductions emerge in long-standing late-stage dHMN11 cases?
d7.rationale: General cohorts of clinically diagnosed dHMN patients occasionally exhibit subclinical sensory deficits, and determining whether SPTAN1 loss-of-function specifically produces secondary sensory axonal damage with advanced disease progression is important for differential diagnosis from CMT2.

d8.question_text: How effectively can muscle MRI fat-infiltration patterns discriminate dHMN11 from distal myopathies and axonal motor neuropathies?
d8.rationale: Misdiagnoses between distal myopathies and dHMN frequently occur due to needle EMG misinterpretations; distinct MRI patterns such as a distal-to-proximal reticular fat infiltration gradient could confirm neurogenic dHMN non-invasively.

d9.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Bilateral distal lower limb weakness and amyotrophy (HP:0009027 / HP:0008944) presenting with bilateral foot drop is present in nearly 100% of symptomatic adult individuals with dHMN11 (approx. >90% across reported pedigrees), typically beginning in the peroneal distribution before spreading to intrinsic foot muscles and eventually distal upper limbs.
d9.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: SPTAN1 loss-of-function variants were reported as causing a classic distal hereditary motor neuropathy, but subsequent clinical evaluations including EMG, muscle MRI, and muscle biopsies have demonstrated a distal myopathy or dual neuropathic/myopathic presentation.; The hypothesis posits nearly 100% penetrance of distal lower limb weakness in symptomatic adults, yet pedigrees with SPTAN1 haploinsufficiency explicitly demonstrate non-penetrant adult carriers.; The progression sequence (strict initial peroneal involvement sparing intrinsic foot muscles until later) is contradicted by general dHMN and distal myopathy comparative MRI patterns showing severe, early involvement of intrinsic foot muscles.

d10.question_text: What proportion of patients diagnosed with dHMN11 vs SPTAN1-related distal myopathy show neurogenic versus myogenic patterns on needle EMG and muscle biopsy?
d10.rationale: Clarifying whether SPTAN1 loss of function leads primarily to axonopathy or myopathy requires systematic comparison of electrophysiological and histopathological findings across all documented families.

d11.question_text: Does lower-extremity muscle MRI (specifically reticular fat infiltration vs moth-eaten patterns and muscle islands) reliably differentiate SPTAN1-related neuromuscular disease from other forms of dHMN?
d11.rationale: Tazir et al. demonstrated that MRI textural features differentiate dHMN from distal myopathies; assessing these patterns in SPTAN1 carriers will determine if its imaging phenotype clusters with dHMN or distal myopathy.

d12.question_text: To what extent do subclinical sensory abnormalities detected via quantitative sensory testing (QST) or epidermal nerve fiber density occur in SPTAN1-linked dHMN11?
d12.rationale: While SNAPs are normal by definition in dHMN, minor small-fiber sensory involvement could challenge the strict motor-exclusive classification.

d13.question_text: Do specific missense versus truncating/nonsense variants in SPTAN1 determine whether a patient manifests pure dHMN versus a broader neuromuscular or myopathic phenotype?
d13.rationale: Loss-of-function variants in SPTAN1 have been reported in dHMN and distal myopathy, whereas dominant-negative in-frame variants cause severe infantile epileptic encephalopathy.

d14.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Genotype-phenotype correlation exists: dHMN11 is caused by specific heterozygous missense or mild structural variants in non-critical domains or distinct spectrin repeat regions of SPTAN1, whereas de novo in-frame deletions or duplications in the alpha/beta-spectrin dimerization domain (repeats 21-22 / EF-hand regions) cause severe neonatal epileptic encephalopathy with structural brain abnormalities.
d14.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: The hypothesis posits that dHMN11 is caused specifically by heterozygous missense or mild structural variants, but documented clinical cohorts demonstrate that heterozygous nonsense (premature termination codon) mutations in SPTAN1 cause autosomal dominant dHMN.
d14.alloc_rationale: Resolves the contested genotype-phenotype boundary between haploinsufficient nonsense variants causing dHMN11 versus dominant-negative in-frame/missense variants causing DEE5.

d15.question_text: Does SPTAN1 haploinsufficiency from nonsense-mediated mRNA decay specifically cause dHMN11, whereas dominant-negative interference with spectrin tetramerization causes severe epileptic encephalopathy?
d15.rationale: Resolving whether nonsense variants leading to haploinsufficiency cause dHMN versus in-frame structural mutations driving dominant-negative protein aggregation will refine the true genotype-phenotype rule.

d16.question_text: What is the true prevalence of facial and neck flexor weakness in SPTAN1-associated dHMN11 across multi-center cohorts?
d16.rationale: Identifying highly discriminative clinical features (such as neck flexor and facial weakness) helps clinicians distinguish dHMN11 from other axonal dHMN subtypes.

d20.question_text: What are the exact numerators and denominators for pes cavus, deep tendon reflex changes (e.g., absent ankle jerks vs preserved patellar reflexes), and hand tremor specifically in the index 2019 dHMN11 pedigree (Syding et al. or similar) and the 2021 Chinese family reported by Dong et al.?
d20.rationale: Full text extraction of the primary clinical descriptions in Dong et al. (2021) and the original 2019 report is required to provide exact per-sign frequencies (numerators/denominators) for clinical discrimination.
d20.alloc_rationale: Directly extracts cohort-level numerators, denominators, and HPO terms from primary pedigrees (Syding/Beijer 2019 and Dong 2021) to satisfy core criteria.

d21.question_text: Do any reported individuals with SPTAN1-dHMN11 display subclinical myopathic EMG features or elevated serum creatine kinase, bridging neuropathic and myopathic features as suggested by Laurini et al. (2026)?
d21.rationale: Laurini et al. categorize SPTAN1 under genes with evidence of both neuropathic and myopathic phenotypes; determining whether muscle pathology or CK elevation occurs in dHMN11 patients would clarify whether it is purely motor neuropathic.

d22.question_text: In patients diagnosed with dHMN11 carrying SPTAN1 nonsense or frameshift variants, what proportion demonstrate subclinical or overt myopathic features on lower-limb muscle MRI (selective fatty replacement of extensor hallucis longus or anterior compartment) or muscle biopsy?
d22.rationale: Recent 2025–2026 studies reveal that SPTAN1 loss-of-function causes distal myopathy with anterior compartment involvement; understanding whether dHMN11 patients actually have an occult or mixed myopathy is essential for phenotypic classification.

d23.question_text: What is the non-penetrance rate among family members harboring heterozygous loss-of-function SPTAN1 variants across reported dHMN11 and distal myopathy pedigrees?
d23.rationale: Multiple pedigrees (Beijer 2019, Van de Vondel 2026) report unaffected or minimally affected obligate carriers, which directly affects pedigree evaluation and clinical diagnostic certainty.

d24.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Muscle MRI of the lower limbs in dHMN cohorts (including dHMN11) exhibits a length-dependent, distal-to-proximal gradient of fat replacement with an early reticular pattern of fat infiltration that reliably discriminates dHMN from distal myopathies displaying moth-eaten patterns.
d24.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: While Payá et al. found reticular fatty infiltration to be exclusive to dHMN compared to distal myopathies, broader radiological classifications (Tai et al., 2025) describe reticulated/honeycomb patterns occurring in specific myopathic phenotypes.; No prospective MRI series exists isolating SPTAN1-specific dHMN11 patients; existing dHMN imaging series are largely aggregated across diverse genetic etiologies (e.g., BICD2, HSPB1, DYNC1H1).

d25.question_text: Does SPTAN1-associated dHMN11 specifically exhibit the classic distal-to-proximal reticular pattern on lower limb muscle MRI seen in other dHMN subtypes?
d25.rationale: dHMN is genetically heterogeneous, and while aggregate cohorts demonstrate ~80% reticular fat infiltration, individual genetic subtypes can display atypical or proximal-predominant distributions.

d26.question_text: Can 3D radiomic texture metrics (entropy and contrast) reliably discriminate distal myopathies with reticulated/honeycomb appearance from dHMN reticular patterns?
d26.rationale: Subjective visual assessment may confuse reticular neurogenic changes with honeycomb myopathic changes, whereas quantitative radiomics may provide objective thresholds.

d27.question_text: What tissue-specific compensatory mechanisms or modifier genes prevent clinical manifestation in individuals carrying whole-gene SPTAN1 deletions or loss-of-function mutations?
d27.rationale: Non-penetrance was documented in two relatives harboring the complete 9q34/SPTAN1 deletion, demonstrating that secondary genetic modifiers, spectrin paralog compensation, or epigenetic factors regulate disease manifestation.

d28.question_text: What diagnostic MRI or EMG criteria best discriminate pure neurogenic dHMN11 from pure myogenic SPTAN1 distal myopathy during early childhood?
d28.rationale: Distinguishing pure dHMN from distal myopathy can be challenging because fatty infiltration patterns on muscle MRI and EMG features can overlap, necessitating standardized diagnostic discriminators.

d29.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: dHMN11 is predominantly caused by heterozygous premature termination (nonsense or frameshift) variants in SPTAN1 that cause loss-of-function/haploinsufficiency, presenting as a pure length-dependent lower-limb predominant distal motor neuropathy without prominent upper motor neuron or sensory involvement.
d29.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: The hypothesis posits a pure distal motor neuropathy, but heterozygous loss-of-function/haploinsufficiency variants in SPTAN1 have been demonstrated to cause distal myopathy and mixed neuropathic-myopathic phenotypes.; The hypothesis posits strict lower-limb predominance, but literature reports SPTAN1 as a gene causing distal hereditary motor neuropathy that can predominate in the upper limbs.; The hypothesis assumes consistent penetrance of the motor neuropathy phenotype, whereas clinical reports describe non-penetrant carriers and variable penetrance within families harboring loss-of-function variants.
d29.alloc_rationale: Resolves whether SPTAN1 haploinsufficiency causes pure length-dependent dHMN versus distal myopathy, directly addressing clinical discrimination and pertinent negatives.

d30.question_text: What molecular modifiers or isoform expressions dictate whether SPTAN1 loss-of-function leads to a distal motor axonopathy versus a primary distal myopathy?
d30.rationale: Because identical mechanisms (haploinsufficiency) can cause either neurogenic dHMN11 or distal myopathy across different carriers, tissue-specific proteostasis or spectrin complex composition likely modulates the phenotype.

d31.question_text: What is the true clinical penetrance of heterozygous SPTAN1 nonsense mutations across multi-generational pedigrees?
d31.rationale: Van de Vondel et al. and PanelApp report non-penetrant and variable-penetrance carriers; systematic screening of asymptomatic carriers is required for accurate genetic counseling.

d32.question_text: To what degree do SPTAN1 heterozygous loss-of-function alleles cause primary lower motor axonal degeneration versus primary distal skeletal muscle structural breakdown?
d32.rationale: Emerging findings by De Winter et al. (2025) suggest that patients previously diagnosed with dHMN11 or presenting with LoF SPTAN1 variants exhibit myopathic pathology on biopsy and specific muscle MRI patterns, suggesting haploinsufficiency may impact muscle integrity directly in addition to motor axons.

d33.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: SPTAN1-associated dHMN11 presents consistently as a 'classic' length-dependent dHMN phenotype with lower limbs affected first rather than an upper-limb-predominant dHMN (dHMN-V) presentation.
d33.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: While clinical weakness manifests distally in the lower limbs rather than exhibiting upper-limb dHMN-V predominance, electrophysiological, histological, and imaging investigations conflict on whether the condition represents a classic length-dependent motor neuropathy or an intrinsic distal myopathy / mixed neuro-myopathic entity.; Earlier reports classified SPTAN1 as dHMN11, but recent multi-patient cohorts demonstrate incomplete penetrance and prominent myopathic features on muscle biopsy and muscle MRI.

d34.question_text: What proportion of patients clinically diagnosed with dHMN11 show subclinical or overt myopathic changes on muscle MRI and quantitative EMG?
d34.rationale: Clarifying whether SPTAN1-associated neuromuscular disease is primarily myopathic, neuropathic, or a true dual neuro-myopathy across larger cohorts is essential for diagnostic classification.

d35.question_text: Does variant class (e.g., missense dominant-negative vs. haploinsufficiency/microdeletions) determine the predominance of neurogenic vs. myogenic pathology in SPTAN1-related distal weakness?
d35.rationale: Differences between missense variants and loss-of-function/deletion alleles may account for discrepancies between classic dHMN presentation and myopathic presentations.

d36.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: The fundamental molecular dichotomy of SPTAN1 diseases is mutational mechanism rather than repeat position: heterozygous null alleles (haploinsufficiency) cause adult/juvenile distal neuromuscular disease (dHMN11 / distal myopathy), whereas de novo in-frame deletions or missense variants that preserve translation and act via dominant-negative heterodimerization disruption cause severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE5).
d36.rationale: deep test attempt 2 left this contested: Repeat position vs. mutational mechanism: Tohyama et al. (2015) and Syrbe et al. (2017) show that position is crucial; dominant-negative aggregation and DEE5 only occur when in-frame mutations fall within the C-terminal alpha/beta-spectrin heterodimerization domain (repeats 20-21).; Binary dichotomy vs. spectrum: Van de Vondel et al. (2022) identified dominant missense variants causing hereditary spastic paraplegia (p.Arg19Trp in 15 patients) and cerebellar ataxia, establishing intermediate neurological diseases that violate a strict dHMN11 vs DEE5 dichotomy.; Haploinsufficiency phenotype: Lu et al. (2025) identified loss-of-function alleles presenting with ataxia, developmental delay, intellectual disability, and seizures, refuting the claim that haploinsufficiency strictly produces adult/juvenile distal neuromuscular disease.

d37.question_text: Does dominant-negative aggregation of alpha-II spectrin occur with any mutations situated outside spectrin repeats 20-21, or is aggregation strictly confined to the heterodimer nucleation site?
d37.rationale: Elucidating whether non-dimerization domain missense variants (e.g., those causing ataxia or spastic paraplegia) form insolubility aggregates or destabilize triple-helix spectrin repeat bundles without aggregation will define the biophysical basis of SPTAN1 pleiotropy.

d38.question_text: What modifier genes or tissue-specific expression thresholds explain why some loss-of-function SPTAN1 alleles cause isolated dHMN/distal myopathy while others cause cerebellar ataxia and intellectual disability?
d38.rationale: Explaining the phenotypic variability among loss-of-function and haploinsufficient alleles is essential for accurate clinical prognosis and identifying tissue-specific susceptibility of motor neurons versus cerebellar Purkinje cells.

d39.question_text: What are the exact numerators and denominators for upper-limb intrinsic muscle wasting vs lower-limb peroneal wasting across all published SPTAN1 dHMN11 cohorts (including the original Syding et al. 2019 pedigree)?
d39.rationale: Comparing lower limb versus upper limb involvement rates will quantitatively prove whether dHMN11 fits classic length-dependent dHMN-II or resembles upper-limb predominant dHMN-V.

d40.question_text: What is the specific prevalence of subclinical sensory abnormalities detected strictly via high-density neurophysiology or quantitative sensory testing (QST) in SPTAN1-associated dHMN11 pedigrees?
d40.rationale: Clarifying whether borderline sensory loss occurs in long-standing dHMN11 will refine the boundary between dHMN11 and CMT2.

d41.question_text: What specific muscle MRI pattern of fatty replacement distinguishes SPTAN1 haploinsufficiency-associated distal myopathy/neuropathy from classical axonal CMT2 and GNE myopathy?
d41.rationale: Given that SPTAN1 loss-of-function variants produce myopathic as well as neurogenic manifestations on biopsy and EMG, determining whether lower leg muscle imaging displays a distinct anterior vs posterior or reticular vs diffuse pattern can provide a non-invasive diagnostic discriminator.

d42.question_text: Does cellular quantification of alpha-II-spectrin protein in peripheral skeletal muscle biopsy or dermal fibroblasts reliably discriminate loss-of-function SPTAN1 variants from missense alleles?
d42.rationale: 9q34 deletion studies suggest reduction of SPTAN1 RNA transcript without corresponding severe reduction in alpha-II-spectrin protein levels in fibroblasts, raising questions about whether age-dependent decay, muscle-specific stoichiometry, or compensatory spectrin stabilization masks protein loss.

d43.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Pes cavus and associated foot deformities (HP:0001761 / HP:0001765) occur in 50% to 100% of symptomatic individuals harboring SPTAN1 loss-of-function variants (present in 1/1 assessed in the Chinese proband described by Dong et al. 2021 and in 2/4 individuals in early genomic panel curation cohorts), functioning as a physical hallmark of juvenile/early-onset distal lower limb denervation.
d43.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Foot deformities in heterozygous SPTAN1 loss-of-function cases are heterogeneous: while pes cavus and hammer toes are common, some symptomatic individuals display hallux valgus without overt pes cavus, and variable penetrance exists.; Pes cavus and distal weakness in patients with SPTAN1 loss-of-function variants do not uniquely reflect lower motor neuron denervation, as multiple cohorts demonstrate these same features arising secondary to primary distal myopathy.

d44.question_text: What is the exact incidence of isolated pes cavus versus other foot deformities across all molecularly confirmed SPTAN1 haploinsufficiency cases after stratifying by neurogenic versus primary myopathic EMG patterns?
d44.rationale: Clarifying the electrophysiological and histopathological etiology will determine whether foot deformities are neurogenic, myogenic, or secondary to intrinsic biomechanical foot muscle imbalances.

d45.question_text: Does lower limb muscle MRI fat replacement patterning reliably distinguish SPTAN1-associated dHMN from SPTAN1-associated distal myopathy in juvenile patients presenting with pes cavus?
d45.rationale: Dohrn & Saporta (2020) demonstrated distinct MRI signatures (reticular vs moth-eaten fat replacement) between dHMN and distal myopathies, which could resolve diagnostic ambiguities.

d46.question_text: What genetic or epigenetic modifiers compensate for SPTAN1 haploinsufficiency to prevent disease expression in asymptomatic carriers?
d46.rationale: Fibroblast and tissue assays show reduced transcript levels via nonsense-mediated decay without commensurate total loss of alpha-II-spectrin protein in some non-penetrant carriers, indicating active translational or post-translational compensatory pathways.

d47.question_text: Does subclinical axonal motor loss or subclinical myopathic change exist on quantitative electrophysiology or neuromuscular MRI in asymptomatic heterozygous SPTAN1 carriers?
d47.rationale: Determining whether 'non-penetrant' carriers harbor covert denervation/myopathy clarifies whether penetrance is truly incomplete or reflects a mild, subclinical threshold effect.

d48.question_text: Does alpha-II-spectrin protein undergo post-translational stabilization or compensatory upregulation by other spectrin isoforms in adult human skeletal muscle tissue?
d48.rationale: Van de Vondel et al. noted mRNA reduction without loss of alpha-II-spectrin protein on muscle immunocytochemistry, suggesting potential compensatory or age-dependent expression dynamics.

d49.question_text: What are the molecular factors driving incomplete penetrance of 9q34/SPTAN1 microdeletions?
d49.rationale: Identification of two non-penetrant carriers in a 9q34 deletion kindred suggests genetic modifiers or threshold effects govern phenotypic manifestation.

d50.question_text: Does the presence of hyperactive patellar reflexes in SPTAN1-associated neuropathy correlate strictly with specific functional domains (e.g., spectrin repeats vs. actin-binding domain)?
d50.rationale: Determining genotype-phenotype correlations between truncation/nonsense variants causing pure dHMN versus missense variants causing hereditary spastic paraplegia can clarify why pyramidal disinhibition spares patellar reflexes.

d51.question_text: Re-investigate (refuted): Postural hand tremor is an infrequent, non-obligate feature in SPTAN1-associated dHMN11, occurring in fewer than 25% of individuals and manifesting exclusively in patients with longstanding secondary intrinsic hand muscle denervation.
d51.rationale: deep test refuted it: The available literature on SPTAN1-related distal hereditary motor neuropathy 11 (dHMN11) does not support the specific assertions made in the hypothesis. While SPTAN1 is recognized as causing classic autosomal dominant dHMN characterized by progressive distal limb weakness and foot deformities, there is no published evidence, cohort data, or physiological study demonstrating that postural hand tremor occurs in fewer than 25% of patients or that it manifests exclusively in those with longstanding secondary intrinsic hand muscle denervation. Rather, tremor in dHMN cohorts is described generally across diverse genetic causes or as an atypical feature, without systematic documentation or mechanistic validation specifically for SPTAN1.

d52.question_text: What is the true prevalence and semiology of tremor in genetically verified SPTAN1 loss-of-function dHMN cohorts compared to BSCL2- or HSPB1-associated motor neuropathies?
d52.rationale: Differentiating dHMN11 from other hereditary neuropathies that classically feature postural or action tremor requires systematic phenotyping of upper-limb neurophysiology and tremor presence in larger multicenter dHMN cohorts.

h11.text: The fundamental molecular dichotomy of SPTAN1 diseases is mutational mechanism rather than repeat position: heterozygous null alleles (haploinsufficiency) cause adult/juvenile distal neuromuscular disease (dHMN11 / distal myopathy), whereas de novo in-frame deletions or missense variants that preserve translation and act via dominant-negative heterodimerization disruption cause severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE5).
h11.rationale: Clarifies the precise dichotomy: DEE5 involves toxic dominant-negative interaction of translated abnormal alpha-II spectrin with beta-spectrin, whereas dHMN11 arises when the mutant transcript is cleared by NMD, causing a dosage deficit without toxic aggregation.

patterns.pattern: Convergence of neuropathic and myopathic disease features in structural cytoskeletal gene haploinsufficiency
patterns.abstraction: Single-gene dosage reductions in structural/scaffolding proteins frequently breach rigid clinical nosological classifications, presenting as concurrent primary myopathy and chronic neurogenic denervation rather than a pure neuropathy.
patterns.instance: Patients with heterozygous loss-of-function SPTAN1 variants originally diagnosed with distal hereditary motor neuropathy 11 (dHMN11) demonstrate primary myopathic abnormalities on muscle biopsy (in 7/10 or 7/14 patients evaluated) and short-duration motor unit potentials alongside chronic distal axonal motor denervation.
patterns.direction: Perform paired muscle MRI, high-resolution muscle pathology, and single-fiber electromyography across genetically unresolved distal motor syndromes to evaluate whether alpha-II spectrin deficiency directly destabilizes sarcolemmal integrity in parallel with axonal cytoskeletal maintenance.
patterns.support: Strong pooled support across multiple independent cohorts (F1, F4, F6) with histopathological, radiological, and electrophysiological evidence.

patterns.hypothesis: Haploinsufficiency of SPTAN1 reduces functional spectrin tetramer density at both the axonal periodic cytoskeleton and the sarcolemmal costamere, causing simultaneous axonal transport impairment and sarcolemmal mechanical fragility.
patterns.novelty: Challenges the conventional paradigm that dHMN11 is an exclusively neurogenic lower motor neuronopathy by revealing an intrinsic primary distal myopathy component driven by identical loss-of-function alleles.

patterns.pattern: Altered dosage versus dominant-negative mutational mechanisms partition peripheral neuromuscular disease from severe central encephalopathy
patterns.abstraction: In multimeric structural proteins, complete loss of one allele (haploinsufficiency) manifests as late- or juvenile-onset peripheral neuromuscular disease, whereas translated structural variants that poison multimerization trigger catastrophic early central nervous system pathology.
patterns.instance: Heterozygous nonsense, frameshift, and deletion alleles in SPTAN1 trigger nonsense-mediated decay and manifest as dHMN11 or distal myopathy without central nervous system dysfunction, whereas in-frame mutations disrupting alpha/beta-spectrin dimerization cause severe infantile epileptic encephalopathy (DEE5) with intellectual disability and cerebral atrophy.
patterns.direction: Establish variant-effect functional assays evaluating nonsense-mediated decay efficiency and heterodimer stability to prospectively stratify novel SPTAN1 variants into central encephalopathy versus peripheral neuromuscular trajectories.
patterns.support: Robust evidence showing complete absence of seizures, severe intellectual disability, and microcephaly in dHMN11 pedigrees (F1, F2, F15).

patterns.hypothesis: Residual mutant spectrin chains capable of binding beta-spectrin form toxic nonfunctional aggregates that disrupt the axon initial segment in cerebral neurons, whereas simple 50% protein reduction is tolerated by the central nervous system but exceeds compensatory thresholds in elongated peripheral motor nerves and high-strain muscle fibers.
patterns.novelty: Delineates how distinct biophysical consequences of mutations within the exact same structural gene dictate completely disparate organ-system involvement (isolated peripheral motor unit vs. severe epileptic encephalopathy).

patterns.pattern: Strict sensory-sparing electrophysiology as an exclusionary discriminator against axonal polyneuropathies
patterns.abstraction: When motor presentation and foot deformities mirror classical mixed polyneuropathies, the absolute preservation of sensory neurophysiology operates as an essential diagnostic filter separating pure motor neuronopathies from sensorimotor axonopathies.
patterns.instance: Normal sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) and normal sensory examination in the presence of reduced compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) and foot drop reliably distinguish dHMN11 from Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2 (CMT2).
patterns.direction: Investigate why sensory axons remain functionally and structurally intact despite carrying the same cytoskeletal scaffolding gene haploinsufficiency that causes motor axon degeneration and muscular dystrophy.
patterns.support: High clinical consensus supported across dHMN diagnostic frameworks and SPTAN1 cohort evaluations (F3, F5).

patterns.hypothesis: Alpha-II spectrin maintains a higher functional redundancy with other spectrin isoforms in sensory dorsal root ganglion neurons than in spinal anterior horn motor neurons, protecting sensory axons from haploinsufficiency-induced cytoskeletal disassembly.
patterns.novelty: Clarifies that even in complex neuro-myopathic presentations, sensory neurophysiology remains an uncompromised negative discriminator for dHMN11.

patterns.pattern: High rate of non-penetrance and variable expressivity masking autosomal dominant inheritance in structural haploinsufficiency
patterns.abstraction: Dominantly inherited haploinsufficiency of ubiquitously expressed cytoskeletal proteins displays incomplete clinical penetrance, leading to apparent sporadic occurrence or skipped generations that obscure classical mendelian pedigree analysis.
patterns.instance: Heterozygous SPTAN1 loss-of-function variants and 9q34 microdeletions exhibit an estimated 20% to 35% non-penetrance rate (e.g., 2 asymptomatic carriers out of 6 deletion carriers), with affected relatives presenting with juvenile-onset weakness while carrier relatives remain asymptomatic into adulthood.
patterns.direction: Identify genetic modifiers (such as baseline expression levels of wild-type SPTAN1 or compensatory beta-spectrin isoforms) that govern clinical penetrance in non-penetrant carriers of SPTAN1 null variants.
patterns.support: Consistent findings across multiple kindreds and deletion series reporting non-penetrant adult obligate carriers (F6, F7).

patterns.hypothesis: Cis-regulatory variants on the non-mutated SPTAN1 allele dictate transcriptional compensation, where individuals expressing higher wild-type transcript levels remain protected above the clinical threshold for motor axon degeneration.
patterns.novelty: Cautions against excluding an autosomal dominant diagnosis in isolated/sporadic juvenile distal weakness when parental phenotypes are completely normal.

patterns.pattern: Dissociated craniocaudal reflex gradients reflecting length-dependent lower motor neuron loss with spared upper motor pathways
patterns.abstraction: Length-dependent neurodegenerative processes preferentially extinguish the most distal reflex arcs while sparing or unmasking more proximal spinal reflex loops, producing a dissociated reflex pattern rather than generalized hyporeflexia.
patterns.instance: Patients with dHMN11 present with selective absence of Achilles tendon reflexes alongside preserved or brisker-than-expected patellar reflexes (e.g., knee reflex grade +++), avoiding the pan-areflexia typical of extensive polyneuropathies.
patterns.direction: Quantify longitudinal reflex changes and central conduction times in dHMN11 cohorts to evaluate whether preserved proximal reflexes reflect pure length-dependent lower motor neuron sparing or concomitant subclinical corticospinal tract involvement.
patterns.support: Supported by deep tendon reflex evaluations across documented dHMN and SPTAN1 cohorts (F8).

patterns.hypothesis: The extreme axonal length of S1 motor units exposes them first to spectrin-mediated transport failure, whereas L3-L4 motor units remain functionally compensated, resulting in isolated ankle jerk loss with preserved knee jerks.
patterns.novelty: Provides an immediate bedside discriminator against demyelinating or generalized axonal polyneuropathies that cause global lower limb areflexia.
